events.summary: Archaeologist Howard Carter and his patron Lord Carnarvon first looked into the sealed tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun. Its largely intact treasures made it one of the most famous archaeological finds of the twentieth century.
NASA launched the Mars Science Laboratory carrying the Curiosity rover. Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in August 2012 to study whether Mars once had environments able to support microbial life.
Alfred Nobel signed his last will at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, leaving most of his fortune to fund annual prizes. The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901.
The Soviet Mars 2 mission's descent capsule crashed onto Mars, making it the first human-made object to reach the planet's surface, even though the landing itself failed.

Twelve men, including Christopher Wren and Robert Boyle, met at Gresham College in London and resolved to found a society to promote experimental learning. It became the Royal Society, one of the oldest scientific academies in existence.
NASA launched Mariner 4 toward Mars. In July 1965 it made the first successful flyby of the planet and sent back the first close-up images of another planet's surface.
Thomas Edison demonstrated his phonograph for the first time, a machine that could record sound and play it back. He had announced the invention eight days earlier.
US Navy officer Richard E. Byrd led an aerial expedition that flew over the South Pole, a milestone of early polar aviation.
The chimpanzee Enos orbited Earth twice aboard Mercury-Atlas 5 and splashed down off Puerto Rico. The flight cleared the way for John Glenn's crewed orbital mission in February 1962.

A meteorite crashed through the roof of a house in Sylacauga, Alabama, and struck a woman napping on her couch, leaving her badly bruised. It remains one of the very few documented cases of a person hit by a meteorite.
OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public as a free research preview. It reached millions of users within weeks and set off a wave of public interest in large language models.
Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, a turning point of the civil rights movement.
A team led by Enrico Fermi achieved the first artificial self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in Chicago Pile-1, a reactor built at the University of Chicago as part of the Manhattan Project.

Space Shuttle Endeavour launched on STS-61, the first servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope. Astronauts installed corrective optics that fixed the blurred vision caused by Hubble's flawed main mirror.
Surgeon Christiaan Barnard led the team that performed the first human-to-human heart transplant, at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The patient, Louis Washkansky, lived for 18 days.
A test engineer sent the world's first SMS text message, 'Merry Christmas', over the Vodafone network in the United Kingdom.
The Observer was first published in London. It is the world's oldest Sunday newspaper.
NASA launched Mars Pathfinder. After landing on July 4, 1997, it deployed Sojourner, the first wheeled rover to operate on Mars.
Ratification of the Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth, ending nationwide Prohibition of alcohol in the United States after almost 14 years.
The Great Smog began in London: cold, still air trapped coal smoke over the city for several days, causing thousands of deaths. It led to Britain's Clean Air Act of 1956.

In Halifax, Nova Scotia, a French cargo ship loaded with explosives collided with another vessel and blew up. The Halifax Explosion was one of the largest human-made explosions before nuclear weapons and killed nearly 2,000 people.
Japanese forces attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The United States declared war on Japan the next day and entered World War II.
Apollo 17 launched on the final Apollo Moon mission. On the way out, the crew photographed the whole sunlit Earth, the image now known as The Blue Marble.

US President Dwight D. Eisenhower delivered his 'Atoms for Peace' speech, proposing international cooperation on peaceful uses of nuclear energy. It helped lead to the founding of the International Atomic Energy Agency in 1957.
Former Beatle John Lennon was shot and killed outside his New York City apartment building, The Dakota.

Douglas Engelbart gave the demonstration later nicknamed 'The Mother of All Demos', publicly debuting the computer mouse, hypertext and a graphical user interface decades before they became mainstream.

The eradication of smallpox was certified after a global vaccination campaign, and the World Health Organization declared the disease eradicated in 1980. The last natural case had been diagnosed in October 1977.
The first Nobel Prize ceremony was held in Stockholm on the fifth anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays, received the first physics prize.
The UN General Assembly, meeting at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The anniversary is observed every year as Human Rights Day.

source.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights - Wikipedia

events.summary: The United Nations established UNICEF, the International Children's Emergency Fund, to provide food and health care to children in countries devastated by World War II.
Apollo 17 landed in the Taurus-Littrow valley, the sixth and final Apollo mission to land astronauts on the Moon.
Guglielmo Marconi received the first transatlantic radio signal, the Morse letter S sent from Cornwall, England, to Signal Hill in Newfoundland.
Nearly 200 parties adopted the Paris Agreement on climate change, committing to hold global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and to pursue a 1.5 degree limit.
Francis Drake set sail from Plymouth, England, on the voyage that made him the first Englishman to circumnavigate the globe. He returned in 1580.
Dutch navigator Abel Tasman became the first recorded European to sight New Zealand.
Roald Amundsen's five-man Norwegian team became the first people to reach the South Pole, about a month ahead of Robert Falcon Scott's British party.
Apollo 17 commander Eugene Cernan climbed back into the lunar module after the mission's third moonwalk. He remains the most recent person to have walked on the Moon.
The first ten amendments to the US Constitution, the Bill of Rights, became law when the Virginia General Assembly ratified them.
The Soviet probe Venera 7 landed on Venus and transmitted data from the surface, the first successful soft landing on another planet.
In the Boston Tea Party, members of the Sons of Liberty dumped chests of British tea into Boston Harbor to protest the Tea Act and taxation without representation.
Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first controlled, powered, heavier-than-air flights near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The first flight lasted about 12 seconds.
The Simpsons premiered as a series with the episode 'Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire'. It became the longest-running American scripted primetime series.
US Secretary of State William Seward proclaimed the adoption of the Thirteenth Amendment, abolishing slavery throughout the United States.
Project SCORE, the world's first communications satellite, was launched. It relayed a recorded Christmas message from President Eisenhower.
Charles Dickens published A Christmas Carol through Chapman & Hall in London. The story of Ebenezer Scrooge helped shape modern Christmas traditions.
Apollo 17 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, ending the last crewed flight to the Moon to date.
The Louisiana Purchase was completed at a ceremony in New Orleans, transferring a vast territory from France and roughly doubling the size of the United States.
Experimental Breeder Reactor I near Arco, Idaho, became the first nuclear power plant to generate electricity, lighting four light bulbs.
Walt Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs premiered at the Carthay Circle Theatre in Los Angeles. It was the first cel-animated feature film.

source.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film) - Wikipedia

events.summary: Apollo 8 launched from Kennedy Space Center, the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth orbit and travel to the Moon.

A fishing trawler landed a strange fish at East London, South Africa. Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer sought expert help, and ichthyologist JLB Smith identified it as a coelacanth, a group known only from fossils and long thought extinct.
John Bardeen and Walter Brattain demonstrated the first working transistor at Bell Labs. With William Shockley, they shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the invention.
Surgeon Joseph Murray and his team in Boston performed the first successful human kidney transplant, between identical twins.
Apollo 8 entered lunar orbit, and astronaut Bill Anders photographed the Earth rising over the Moon's horizon, the famous Earthrise image.
Europe's first Ariane rocket launched successfully from Kourou, French Guiana.
Isaac Newton was born in Woolsthorpe, England, by the Julian calendar then used in England. His laws of motion and gravitation laid the foundations of classical physics.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched on an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana. Its infrared instruments observe some of the earliest galaxies in the universe.
Marie and Pierre Curie announced to the French Academy of Sciences that they had found a new radioactive element, which they named radium.
A magnitude 9.1 to 9.3 undersea earthquake off Sumatra triggered tsunamis across the Indian Ocean, killing more than 200,000 people in over a dozen countries.
Charles Darwin set sail aboard HMS Beagle. Observations from the five-year voyage, including in the Galápagos Islands, later shaped his theory of evolution by natural selection.
The International Monetary Fund was created when 29 nations signed its founding agreement, part of the postwar international financial system.
Galileo recorded Neptune in his notes while observing Jupiter but mistook it for a fixed star. Neptune was not identified as a planet until 1846.
The Lumière brothers screened films for their first paying audience at the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines in Paris, a landmark in the birth of cinema.
US Army troops killed hundreds of Lakota men, women and children at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota.

Richard Feynman gave his lecture 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom' at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, imagining the manipulation of matter atom by atom. It is often cited as an inspiration for nanotechnology.

source.title: There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom - Wikipedia

events.summary: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formally established. It lasted until its dissolution in December 1991.
Thomas Edison gave the first public demonstration of his incandescent lighting system at his laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey.
The United States transferred control of the Panama Canal to Panama, under treaties signed in 1977.
Astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi discovered Ceres from Palermo, Sicily. It was the first asteroid found and is now classified as a dwarf planet.
ARPANET officially switched to the TCP/IP protocols, a cutover often described as the birth of the modern internet.
The Soviet Union launched Luna 1, the first spacecraft to reach the vicinity of the Moon and the first to go into orbit around the Sun.
The 36-inch Great Lick Refractor on Mount Hamilton, California, saw first light. It was the world's largest refracting telescope until 1897.
China's Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon and later deployed the Yutu-2 rover.
Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, fell back into Earth's atmosphere and burned up, about three months after its launch in October 1957.
NASA's Spirit rover landed on Mars. Planned for a 90-day mission, it kept exploring for more than six years.
The Ford Motor Company announced an eight-hour workday and a minimum daily wage of $5, roughly doubling pay for many of its workers.
Construction began on the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. It opened in 1937 as the world's longest suspension bridge span at the time.
Alfred Vail and colleagues, working with Samuel Morse, demonstrated a telegraph that sent messages as patterns of dots and dashes, the forerunner of Morse code.
Geophysicist Alfred Wegener first presented his theory of continental drift. Long rejected, it was vindicated by plate tectonics in the 1960s.
Galileo first observed the moons of Jupiter through his telescope, initially taking them for fixed stars. Their motion around Jupiter undermined the idea that everything orbits Earth.
The first transatlantic commercial telephone service opened between New York City and London, carried by radio.
Galileo Galilei died at his villa near Florence, where he had spent his last years under house arrest after his trial by the Inquisition.
Herman Hollerith received a US patent for his punched-card method for tabulating statistics. His machines processed the 1890 US census, and his company became part of IBM.
Jean-Pierre Blanchard became the first person to fly in a balloon in the United States, lifting off from Philadelphia.
Steve Jobs introduced the original iPhone at the Macworld conference in San Francisco.
The US Army's Project Diana bounced radar signals off the Moon and detected the echoes, the first radar contact with another celestial body.
The United Nations General Assembly held its first meeting, at Methodist Central Hall in Westminster, London.
Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with diabetes in Toronto, became the first person to be treated with an injection of insulin.
US Surgeon General Luther Terry released the report 'Smoking and Health', which concluded that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men and launched decades of anti-smoking policy.
A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince, Haiti, devastating the capital and killing more than 100,000 people by most estimates.
A German test pilot made the first use of an aircraft ejection seat, escaping from a Heinkel He 280 jet fighter.
Johnny Cash performed live at Folsom State Prison in California. The recording became one of his best-known albums.
The US Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris with Great Britain, formally ending the American Revolutionary War.
The European Huygens probe, carried by NASA's Cassini spacecraft, landed on Saturn's moon Titan. It is still the only landing ever made in the outer Solar System.
Wikipedia went online, launched by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger as a free encyclopedia that anyone can edit.
After bird strikes disabled both engines, US Airways Flight 1549 glided to a landing on the Hudson River in New York. All 155 people on board were rescued.
Members of Ernest Shackleton's Antarctic expedition reached the area of the South Magnetic Pole.
Space Shuttle Columbia launched on mission STS-107. It broke apart during re-entry on February 1, 2003, killing all seven crew members.
Captain James Cook led the first expedition known to sail south of the Antarctic Circle.
Robert Falcon Scott's British party reached the South Pole, only to find that Roald Amundsen had arrived a month earlier. Scott and his companions died on the return journey.
James Cook became the first known European to reach the Hawaiian Islands, which he named the Sandwich Islands.
The Paris Peace Conference opened at Versailles to settle the terms ending World War I, leading to the Treaty of Versailles.
Apple introduced the Lisa, one of the first personal computers with a graphical user interface to be sold commercially. Its high price limited sales, but its ideas shaped the Macintosh.
NASA launched the New Horizons probe. On July 14, 2015, it made the first flyby of Pluto, revealing mountains of water ice and vast nitrogen-ice plains.
John F. Kennedy was inaugurated as US president. His address urged Americans to 'ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.'

source.title: Inauguration of John F. Kennedy - Wikipedia

events.summary: The USS Nautilus, the world's first nuclear-powered submarine, was launched in Groton, Connecticut.
Concorde began commercial supersonic passenger service, with flights from London to Bahrain and from Paris to Rio de Janeiro.
On Bloody Sunday in Saint Petersburg, imperial troops fired on peaceful marchers bringing a petition to the Tsar. The massacre helped ignite the Russian Revolution of 1905.
Apple's '1984' commercial for the Macintosh, directed by Ridley Scott, aired nationally during Super Bowl XVIII. It is often ranked among the most influential TV ads ever made.
Elizabeth Blackwell received her medical degree from Geneva Medical College in New York, becoming the first woman to earn an MD in the United States.
Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh piloted the bathyscaphe Trieste to a depth of about 10,900 meters in the Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the ocean.
James W. Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill near Sacramento, setting off the California Gold Rush.
Apple released the original Macintosh at a price of $2,495, bringing the mouse-driven graphical interface to a mass market.
Voyager 2 made its closest approach to Uranus. It remains the only spacecraft ever to visit the planet.
The first Winter Olympic Games opened in Chamonix, France. Sixteen nations competed in events such as skiing, skating and ice hockey over eleven days.
NASA's Opportunity rover landed on Mars at Meridiani Planum. Planned for a 90-day mission, it kept driving and sending data for more than fourteen years.
The British First Fleet entered Sydney Cove under Captain Arthur Phillip, founding the penal colony of New South Wales. The date is marked today as Australia Day.
The Constitution of India came into effect, making India a republic with Rajendra Prasad as its first president. The day is celebrated as Republic Day.
Soviet troops liberated the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration and extermination camp in occupied Poland. The anniversary is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
A cabin fire during a launch rehearsal for Apollo 1 killed astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee. NASA redesigned the command module before any crew flew again.
Jane Austen's novel Pride and Prejudice was first published in London. It was issued anonymously, credited only to the author of Sense and Sensibility.
The Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing its seven crew members. The cause was a failed O-ring seal in a solid rocket booster in cold weather.
Edgar Allan Poe's poem The Raven was published in the New York Evening Mirror. It made Poe famous almost overnight.
Karl Benz applied for a patent on his gasoline-powered Motorwagen in Germany. It is widely regarded as the first practical automobile.
Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany by President Paul von Hindenburg. Within months the Nazi government had dismantled the Weimar Republic's democracy.
Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated in New Delhi by Nathuram Godse. Gandhi had led India's nonviolent independence movement for decades.
The United States House of Representatives passed the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery. It was ratified by the states in December of that year.
Explorer 1, the first satellite of the United States, was launched from Cape Canaveral. Its instruments detected the Van Allen radiation belts around Earth.

Four Black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter at Woolworth's in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave. The sit-ins spread across the South and helped end segregation in restaurants.
The Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart over Texas while returning to Earth, killing all seven astronauts. Foam that struck the wing at launch had damaged its heat shield.
Mexico and the United States signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, ending the Mexican-American War. Mexico ceded about half of its territory, including California.
James Joyce's novel Ulysses was published in Paris by Sylvia Beach's bookshop Shakespeare and Company. It became a landmark of modernist literature.
A small plane crash in Iowa killed musicians Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J. P. Richardson. The loss was later called the day the music died.
The Soviet probe Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon. It sent back the first photographs taken from the lunar surface.
Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin met at Yalta in Crimea. They planned the final defeat of Germany and the shape of postwar Europe.
Mark Zuckerberg and fellow Harvard students launched the social network that became Facebook. It opened to the general public in 2006.
Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith founded the film studio United Artists. It let actors and directors control and distribute their own work.
Apollo 14 landed on the Moon with Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell. Shepard famously hit two golf balls on the lunar surface.
Elizabeth II became queen of the United Kingdom on the death of her father, George VI. She reigned for seventy years, longer than any other British monarch.
A plane carrying the Manchester United football team crashed on take-off in Munich, killing 23 people. Eight of the dead were players.
The Beatles arrived at New York's newly renamed John F. Kennedy airport, starting their first visit to the United States. Their arrival marked the start of the British Invasion in American pop music.
Astronaut Bruce McCandless made the first untethered spacewalk, flying a jet-powered Manned Maneuvering Unit away from the Space Shuttle Challenger.
The Boy Scouts of America was incorporated by William D. Boyce. It grew into one of the largest youth organizations in the United States.
The NASDAQ stock market began trading as the world's first electronic stock exchange. Quotes were shown on computer screens rather than called out on a trading floor.
The Beatles made their first appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show. About 73 million people watched, a record for American television at the time.
The Boeing 747 made its first flight. The wide-body jumbo jet made long-distance air travel far cheaper.
The Treaty of Paris ended the Seven Years' War. France ceded Canada to Britain, reshaping colonial North America.
IBM's chess computer Deep Blue defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in a game under tournament conditions for the first time. Kasparov still won that match; Deep Blue won the 1997 rematch.
Nelson Mandela walked free after 27 years in prison in South Africa. Four years later he was elected the country's first Black president.
Scientists of the LIGO and Virgo collaborations announced the first direct detection of gravitational waves. The signal came from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away.
George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue premiered in New York with Gershwin at the piano. It blended jazz with classical concert music.
NASA's NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft touched down on the asteroid 433 Eros. It was the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid.
Galileo Galilei arrived in Rome to face the Inquisition for supporting the view that the Earth moves around the Sun. He was later convicted and spent his last years under house arrest.
France tested its first atomic bomb, code-named Gerboise Bleue, in the Algerian Sahara. France became the fourth country with nuclear weapons.
Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray both filed telephone documents with the US Patent Office on the same day. Bell received the patent, which led to years of legal disputes.
Voyager 1 turned its camera back toward the inner Solar System and took the photo of Earth later called the Pale Blue Dot. It was about six billion kilometres from home.
Canada adopted its red and white maple leaf flag. It replaced the Red Ensign, which included the British Union Jack.
A meteor about 20 metres across exploded in the sky over Chelyabinsk, Russia. Its shock wave shattered windows and injured about 1,500 people.
Howard Carter opened the sealed burial chamber of Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Inside was the king's sarcophagus, still intact.
Fidel Castro became Prime Minister of Cuba, weeks after the revolution that ousted Fulgencio Batista. He led the country for nearly five decades.
The philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake in Rome for heresy. Among his views was that stars are distant suns with their own planets.
The United States launched Vanguard 2, the first satellite designed to measure cloud cover from orbit. It was an early forerunner of weather satellites.
Clyde Tombaugh at Lowell Observatory in Arizona discovered Pluto by comparing photographic plates. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater on Mars. It carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which later made the first powered flight on another planet.
Thomas Edison was granted a patent for the phonograph, the first machine that could record and play back sound.
The Soviet Union launched the core module of the Mir space station. Mir was occupied almost continuously for about ten years.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art opened in New York City. It became the largest art museum in the United States.
John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, circling it three times in the Friendship 7 capsule.
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto in London. It became one of the most influential political texts ever written.
President Richard Nixon arrived in Beijing for a week-long visit to China. The trip opened relations between the two countries after decades of hostility.
The United States men's ice hockey team, mostly college players, beat the heavily favoured Soviet team at the Lake Placid Winter Olympics. The upset became known as the Miracle on Ice.
Scientists at the Roslin Institute in Scotland announced the birth of Dolly the sheep. She was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.
US Marines raised the American flag on Mount Suribachi during the Battle of Iwo Jima. The photograph of the second flag-raising became one of the most famous images of the war.
Light from supernova SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud reached Earth. It was the closest supernova seen in nearly four centuries.
Pope Gregory XIII issued the papal bull Inter gravissimas, which introduced the Gregorian calendar. Ten days were dropped to bring the calendar back in step with the seasons.
Astronomers at Cambridge announced the discovery of the first pulsar, a rapidly rotating neutron star. Jocelyn Bell Burnell had spotted its regular radio pulses months earlier.
Hiram Revels of Mississippi took his seat in the US Senate, becoming the first African American to serve in Congress.
Cassius Clay, soon to be known as Muhammad Ali, defeated Sonny Liston to become world heavyweight boxing champion.
Napoleon escaped from exile on the island of Elba and returned to France. His comeback ended at Waterloo about four months later.
Robert Watson-Watt's team showed that a bomber could be detected by the radio waves it reflected. The Daventry experiment led to Britain's radar network.
The Reichstag, Germany's parliament building in Berlin, was set on fire. The Nazi government used the fire as a pretext to suspend civil liberties.
Martin Kamen and Sam Ruben discovered carbon-14 at the University of California, Berkeley. The isotope later made radiocarbon dating possible.
Francis Crick and James Watson worked out the double-helix structure of DNA at Cambridge. Their paper, published that April, relied on X-ray images from Rosalind Franklin.
Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme was shot dead while walking home from a cinema in Stockholm. The case remained officially unsolved for 34 years.
Stranded in Jamaica, Christopher Columbus used a predicted lunar eclipse to persuade local people to keep supplying his crew with food.
Hattie McDaniel won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for Gone with the Wind. She was the first African American to win an Oscar.
Yellowstone was established as the first national park in the world by a law signed by President Ulysses S. Grant.
The Soviet probe Venera 3 crashed onto Venus, the first spacecraft to reach the surface of another planet. Its communications had failed before arrival.
The US Air Force bomber Lucky Lady II landed in Texas after the first nonstop flight around the world. It was refuelled in the air four times.
The supersonic airliner Concorde made its first test flight, from Toulouse in France. It entered passenger service in 1976.
Georges Bizet's opera Carmen premiered at the Opéra-Comique in Paris. Its first reception was cool, but it became one of the most performed operas.
The United States adopted The Star-Spangled Banner as its national anthem by an act of Congress.
The first Congress of the United States met in New York City under the newly ratified Constitution. It lacked a quorum and could not begin business until April.
Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated as US president during the Great Depression. In his address he said the only thing to fear is fear itself.
Winston Churchill gave a speech in Fulton, Missouri, warning that an iron curtain had descended across Europe. The phrase came to define the Cold War divide.
NASA's Voyager 1 made its closest approach to Jupiter. Its images revealed active volcanoes on the moon Io.
Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table was presented to the Russian Chemical Society. He left gaps for elements not yet discovered and predicted their properties.
Aspirin was registered as a trademark by the German company Bayer. Acetylsalicylic acid became one of the most widely used drugs in the world.
Alexander Graham Bell was granted a US patent for the telephone. It became one of the most valuable patents ever issued.
State troopers attacked civil rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama. Bloody Sunday helped push the Voting Rights Act through Congress.
Protests by women textile workers in Petrograd on International Women's Day grew into the February Revolution. Within a week the Russian monarchy had fallen.
Philips demonstrated a prototype compact disc player to the press in the Netherlands. The CD, developed with Sony, went on sale in 1982.
The Barbie doll made its debut at the American International Toy Fair in New York. It became one of the best-selling toys in history.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 9 carrying the dog Chernushka and a mannequin. It was a final test of the Vostok spacecraft before Yuri Gagarin's flight.
Alexander Graham Bell made the first successful telephone call, saying to his assistant: Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.
Astronomers watching Uranus pass in front of a star discovered that the planet has rings. They saw the star blink several times before and after it.
Lithuania declared its independence from the Soviet Union, the first Soviet republic to do so.
A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off northeastern Japan triggered a tsunami that killed about 18,000 people. It also caused meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant.
Mahatma Gandhi began the Salt March to the Arabian Sea in protest against the British salt tax. The 24-day march drew worldwide attention to Indian independence.
Tim Berners-Lee submitted his proposal for an information management system at CERN. It became the World Wide Web.
William Herschel discovered Uranus from his garden in Bath, England. It was the first planet found with a telescope.
Tsar Alexander II of Russia, who had abolished serfdom, was assassinated by a bomb in Saint Petersburg.
Eli Whitney was granted a patent for the cotton gin. It made cotton far more profitable and deepened the South's reliance on slavery.
The Gold Standard Act made gold the sole standard for redeeming paper money in the United States.
Julius Caesar was stabbed to death by a group of Roman senators led by Brutus and Cassius. The date became known as the Ides of March.
Symbolics.com became the first registered .com internet domain name. Domain registration was free and handled by hand at the time.
Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket in Auburn, Massachusetts. It flew for about two and a half seconds and reached 12 metres.
Gemini 8, with Neil Armstrong and David Scott, made the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit. A stuck thruster forced an early emergency return.
The United States launched Vanguard 1, the first satellite powered by solar cells. It is the oldest human-made object still in orbit.
The 14th Dalai Lama fled Lhasa in disguise during the Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule. He reached exile in India two weeks later.
A British court in India sentenced Mahatma Gandhi to six years in prison for sedition. He was released after two years on health grounds.
Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, spending about twelve minutes outside the Voskhod 2 capsule.
Pluto was photographed for the first time at Lowell Observatory, but nobody recognized it as a planet. It was identified fifteen years later.
The Sydney Harbour Bridge was officially opened. Its steel arch was the widest long-span bridge in the world at the time.
Harriet Beecher Stowe's anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom's Cabin was published in book form. It became the best-selling novel of the nineteenth century.
Albert Einstein's paper setting out his general theory of relativity was published in the journal Annalen der Physik.
The federal prison on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay closed. It had been too costly to run.
Jack Dorsey sent the first message on the service that became Twitter. The service launched to the public that July.
Auguste and Louis Lumière showed their first film, workers leaving their factory in Lyon, to a private audience in Paris.
Arthur Schawlow and Charles Townes received a US patent for the laser's design, then called an optical maser. The first working laser followed that May.
The abbreviation OK first appeared in print in the Boston Morning Post, as a joke spelling of oll korrect. It became one of the most widely used words in the world.
President Ronald Reagan proposed the Strategic Defense Initiative, a plan for space-based defences against nuclear missiles. Critics nicknamed it Star Wars.
Robert Koch announced in Berlin that he had found the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. The date is now World Tuberculosis Day.
The tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground in Prince William Sound, Alaska, spilling about 41 million litres of crude oil. It became one of the worst environmental disasters in US history.
Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan, the largest moon of Saturn. It was the first moon found orbiting a planet other than Earth and Jupiter.
Six European countries signed the Treaty of Rome, creating the European Economic Community. It grew into today's European Union.
Jonas Salk announced on national radio that he had successfully tested a vaccine against polio. A mass trial in 1954 confirmed it worked.
Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty at the White House, witnessed by President Jimmy Carter. Egypt became the first Arab state to recognize Israel.
Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León sighted the coast of Florida. He named it after the Easter season, Pascua Florida.
The US Food and Drug Administration approved sildenafil, sold as Viagra. The drug had first been tested for heart chest pain.
The Turkish cities of Constantinople and Angora were officially renamed Istanbul and Ankara.
A reactor at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania partly melted down. It was the most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power.
Pharmacist John Pemberton brewed the first batch of Coca-Cola in Atlanta, Georgia. It was first sold as a medicinal tonic.
NASA's Mariner 10 made the first flyby of Mercury, photographing its cratered surface. It was also the first probe to use a gravity assist from another planet.
Georgia doctor Crawford Long used ether as an anaesthetic to remove a tumour from a patient's neck. It was among the first operations under general anaesthesia.
The United States agreed to buy Alaska from Russia for 7.2 million dollars. Critics mocked it as Seward's Folly.
The Eiffel Tower was inaugurated in Paris for the World's Fair. At 300 metres it was the tallest structure in the world.
Daylight saving time took effect in the United States for the first time, as a wartime measure to save fuel.
